newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia editors less effusive than leaders on Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Asia editors less effusive than leaders on Clinton.

text.p: Editors of Asian newspapers were less enthusiastic than their leaders about Bill Clinton's re-election as U.S. president, expressing cautious hope that he would focus more on Asia.

In editorials on Thursday some were critical of the campaign and the vote, saying Americans had opted for the status quo, while others expressed relief that Clinton's re-election would bring continuity to U.S. foreign policy in the region.

"To put it simply, the region is looking for something dynamic that would be the watershed of American policy towards the region," Kavi Chongkittavorn, executive editor of Thailand's The Nation said in an editorial.
The tone of editorials was more cautious than the mostly effusive reaction from Asian leaders, most of whom said Clinton's win could only help regional stability.
Instead they reflected some of the weaknesses underlying Clinton's largely positive image in Asia, including Washington's relations with China, the tense Korean peninsula and trade.

South Korean newspapers took the Clinton administration to task for what they said was its readiness to maintain a 1994 agreement with North Korea, enabling the latter to seek concessions at the expense of security on the peninsula.

"Clinton's policy towards the Korean peninsula should be sought under the principles of the international community in the future," the Chosun Ilbo said in an editorial. Under the 1994 accord, North Korea agreed to freeze its suspected nuclear arms programme in return for safer light-water reactors.

The Singapore Straits Times said it hoped that by not having to worry about re-election, Clinton should have more freedom in policy initiatives, particularly with China, which has been at odds with Washington on issues ranging from trade to Taiwan.
It called for him to take on more Asia-literate advisers and chided him for failing to take up invitations to visit Beijing.
It expressed hope for "an even-handed policy towards China, as this strategic relationship is going to determine the shape of geopolitics well into the next century.
State newspapers in China itself were also cautiously optimistic, noting the repeated diplomatic clashes of the last four years but looking forward to new stability.
"Various obstacles in Sino-U.S. relations will hopefully ease and be resolved during Clinton's second term," said the Business News of Shanghai in a front page analysis.
Newspapers in India, which has locked horns with Washington over its nuclear programme and Kashmir, were less hopeful.
Many ridiculed Clinton, doubting he could brush aside the domestic scandals dogging his first term to achieve greatness overseas. Others dismissed his foreign policy as a sham.

"If his first term is any indication, there is nothing Clinton loves more than playing globo-cop, if only to distract attention from domestic irritants. The time for such puerile diplomacy is over," the Indian Express said.
But elsewhere, the tone was one of relief. Australian papers said the U.S. electorate had voted for a pragmatic presidency and what the Financial Review called a "fine balance".

The Australian newspaper headlined its editorial "U.S. votes for sensible status quo", and said Clinton's re-election and Republican control of the Congress was good news for the "international strategic and trade environment".
The Bangkok Post agreed, saying the United States under Clinton had been a "decent superpower", treating nations with dignity through "steady, if seldom spectacular" foreign policy.

"We always have valued the presence of the United States in a potential power vacuum in Asia, and particularly in Southeast Asia. Japan and China, with their imposing economic and military mights respectively, need the power balance which the U.S, provides in the region," the Thai English-language paper said.
Others predicted a downside to this, saying Clinton may take a tougher stance on issues such as human rights.
The Jakarta Post said his re-election gave continuity to Indonesian-U.S. relations but added Clinton was likely to get tougher on a number of issues now he was firmly back in power.

Washington has pursued a middle course in its ties with Indonesia, developing closer relations with the world's most populous Moslem nation while balancing domestic pressures over the country's human rights record.
